title: Is AI killing commercial engines for indie developers?
author: SecureReindeer3989
selftext:
As a gameplay engineer, I have been using Unity and Unreal both professionally and on personal projects.
I have been using AI more and more in my workflow, but what surprises me the most is how my workflow is changing.

Instead of using tools inside unity for level design, I instead use Blender for superior ease of use and custom tooling. I generate extra geo in Blender on export and setup all shaders/textures on import, a workflow that is very customized to the game I'm making.
This to get a look I otherwise would not have done/been able to.

Now I'm testing Godot in some smaller prototype projects and I have never even opened the editor. There has so far been no need. I'm sure I will at some point when I am actually going to make things look the way I want them, but that is not my point.

What I'm seeing is that I could just as well skip using Unity/Unreal/Godot for a fully customized engine, something I would never have thought of before due to the amount of extra work.

Why do I need highly complicated code that is designed for a massive number of use cases?
Is AI killing commercial engines for indie developers? I'm thinking this is what is going to happen soon.

replies.author: Senior-Mistake9927
replies.body:
They absolutely are.

In software engineering, a platform is any foundational layer that provides a stable API, runtime environment, and toolchain for higher-level applications to run on.

Also on "far more time and resources than the game itself." That's only true if you fall into the trap of trying to build a general-purpose engine that can be used to make any genre of games. The cost/profit analysis in making a narrow purpose built engine for a specific set of games depends entirely on how many of them you are intending to make with it. If you're only making 1, then yeah, it costs more. But if you're planning a series, or will be reusing it to make other games of the same genre?. It's worth it.

comments.author: TechgeekOne
comments.body:
You're just further making my point that the view is naive.
 - Streaming is required to avoid frame hitching, whether you think it's necessary or not it's in fact necessary if you cannot fit the entire level or game into memory on load. Fact is there are very hard limits on how much you can load and how quickly, and almost every single game runs into this. A game that locks up for 10 seconds (which is short btw) is a bad experience for the player.
 - "just clear everything" is the same problem. It's incredibly wasteful and slow to reload things from disk and you still need to keep some things loaded to display a loading animation.
 - None of that negates the build system, asset handling, or animation points. Every single game needs those in some form.

The only point you're making here is that you really don't understand what's happening under the hood.

comments.author: Economy_Bedroom3902
comments.body:
The engine's visual editor is a tool that's suited to manual configuration of the game's world's/scenes.  If you were building a minecraft clone before the era of AI, you also weren't using the visual editor, because the procedural gen code was populating the visual elements.  Nothing was ever hand placed.

I DO think indie devs will be more willing to roll their own engines now...  But I don't think the big engines are going anywhere because even in the new world they have a bunch of advantages:
- standardized multiplayer libs
- standardized audio and render pipelines
- standardized control config systems
- mature tooling for things like ecs and cross lang compiling
- easier console support

The other big thing...  Your AI agent can find a thousand examples of open source unity or unreal projects in it's training data and web searches.  So it tends to do "best practices" for those types of projects more naturally.  If you build your own engine and you don't understand the implications of the choices you let the AI make, you can pretty easily make a game that will only work on a specific model of macbook, and is virtually impossible to get working elsewhere.
